extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of classical mechanics; readers of Newton's Principia
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the individual propositions, corollaries, and demonstrations from Newton's Principia in this chunk, focusing on laws and quantitative relations for oscillations, fluid resistance, and efflux. Each entry records the theorem statement and surrounding explanatory guidance/corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries (resistance ↔ gravity; maxima; local velocity)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Corol. 1–3 after preceding proposition) The resistance at the lowest point C is to the weight (gravity) as the area {OP ÷ OQ} IEF is to the area PINM; the resistance is maximal where area PIHR is to IEF as OR to OQ; the local velocity at points is inversely proportional to the resistance, and at the initial motion equals the velocity of the same body oscillating in the same cycloid without any resistance (in half ratio of resistance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corollaries follow from the area construction used to represent resisting forces and gravity: area representing resistance is comparable to the area representing gravity, so ratios of those areas give ratios of resistance to gravity; maxima occur where the moment (PIGR - Y) vanishes. The corollaries note practical difficulties of computation and motivate the next, more general proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX (Theorem XXIII) — cycloid oscillation area law
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line aB equals the arc of the cycloid described by an oscillating body, and at each point D perpendiculars DK are erected which are to the length of the pendulum as the body's resistance at the arc points is to gravity, then the difference between the whole arc described in descent and the whole subsequent arc described in ascent, multiplied by the semisum of those arcs, is equal (as nearly as possible) to the area occupied by all the perpendiculars DK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: represent velocities from vacuum by perpendiculars DE, de; represent resistances by DK proportional to pendulum length; relate infinitesimal decrements and increments of velocity through similar triangles; sum products to obtain equality of the rectangular area Aa × ½aB with the area made by perpendiculars DK (area BKTa). Corollary: from this law one may deduce the ratio of resistance to gravity at the middle point, and special cases when resistance is uniform, proportional to velocity, or proportional to square of velocity give approximate numerical relations (e.g., if resistance ∝ velocity then the figure approximates an ellipse and yields particular ratios like 7/11 Aa to pendulum length; if ∝ v^2 the figure approximates a parabola leading to different numerical factors). Scholium: these conclusions are practically accurate despite approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI (Theorem XXIV) — monotonic relation of resistance and arc-difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If the resistance of an oscillating body at each part of the described arcs increases or decreases in a given ratio, then the difference between the arc described in descent and the subsequent arc described in ascent will increase or decrease in the same ratio (approximately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: the difference of arcs originates from the pendulum's retardation by the medium's resistance, so the difference is proportional to the total retardation and hence to the resisting force. In the previous proposition a rectangle proportional to aB and the resistance represented the arc-difference Aa; thus Aa varies as the resistance. Corollaries: if resistance ∝ velocity then arc-difference ∝ total arc; if resistance ∝ v^2 then arc-difference ∝ (total arc)^2; generally, for any power law of velocity the same power law holds between resistance and arc-difference. Mixed laws produce mixed contributions accordingly; the law for resistance as a function of velocity is the same as that for the difference as a function of arc length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXII (Theorem XXV) — similarity scaling for systems of particles
rubrics_metrics.description: If two systems each consist of equal numbers of similar particles placed correspondingly, and have a given ratio of densities, and if they begin to move similarly with times proportional (the corresponding particles moving in times proportional), and if particles in the same system do not touch except at reflection moments nor attract/repel except by accelerative forces proportional to inverse diameters of corresponding particles and to squares of velocities, then corresponding particles in the two systems will continue to move similarly in proportional times (and conversely).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a similarity (scaling) principle: when initial configurations and interparticle force laws scale appropriately (forces ∝ diameter^{-1} and ∝ v^2), overall motions remain similar and times scale. Corollaries: if two bodies similar and proportionally situated are projected into two similar elastic fluids whose parts correspond in size and density, and driving forces scale as projectile diameters^{-1} and v^2, then motions and distances remain proportionally similar in proportional times. This underpins later scaling of resistance laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIII (Theorem XXVI) — composite law for resistance of system parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same hypotheses, the resistances on corresponding larger parts of the systems are in a composite ratio made of the duplicate (square) ratio of their velocities, the duplicate (square) ratio of their diameters, and the ratio of the densities of the system parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: resistance arises partly from centripetal/centrifugal forces among particles (proportional to total accelerating forces and mass) — giving ∝ v^2 and inversely to interparticle distance (hence ∝ diam^{-2} when recast), and partly from collisions/reflections (numbers of reflections ∝ v and inversely to spacing; reflection forces ∝ v × size^3 × density), so combining yields resistance ∝ v^2 × diameter^2 × density (text presents the composite reasoning). Corollaries elaborate consequences: in elastic gases resistance of fast projectiles ≈ ∝ v^2; for similar projectiles in same density fluids and very high speed resistances scale as diameter^2; for non-fully-elastic microscopic interactions or non-lubric particle behavior, resistance departs from exact v^2 law and is larger; diminution of particle-scale centrifugal effects causes less accurate v^2 scaling for larger bodies; finer-particle media restore the squared-velocity law more accurately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXIV (Theorem XXVII) — extension to contacting particles (high lubrication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conclusions of the two preceding propositions (similarity and composite resistance laws) hold even when the particles of the systems touch one another, provided those particles are extremely lubricous (i.e., contact forces vanish except as limiting cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By imagining interparticle repulsive forces that blow up near contact and vanish rapidly upon separation, and compressing systems so particles nearly touch, motions approach those of non-contacting particles; differences can be made arbitrarily small by decreasing interparticle gaps. Corollaries: same scaling/resistance laws apply when systems' parts are in contact but extremely lubricous; consequence for fluids with contacting but lubricious particles — resistance still scales compositely, and in elastic-fluid limit projectiles obey v^2 resistance, while departure from lubrication increases resistance beyond v^2 scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXV (Theorem XXVIII) — sphere vs cylinder resistance relation
rubrics_metrics.description: If a globe (sphere) and a cylinder of equal diameters move with equal very great velocities in a rare elastic medium along the cylinder axis, then the resistance experienced by the globe is half (duplo minor) that of the cylinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof models the medium as particles impinging and reflecting; comparing effectiveness of a particle's impact on sphere vs cylinder via similar triangles shows per-particle effect scales as BE^2:BC^2, integrate over surface to compare total effect. The solid determining the total effect for the sphere is a paraboloid occupying half the solid for the cylinder, hence sphere's resistance ≈ 1/2 cylinder's. Scholium: the same method compares other shapes to find shapes of least resistance for given base and height (applications to ship hull design); formulas and constructions for minimal-resistance frustum and other revolved profiles are given. Also provided is a parametric criterion for shapes whose revolutions minimize resistance relative to circular solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVI (Problem VIII) — resistance of a sphere in a rare elastic fluid at very high speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive method: extend radius CA to points S and R so that AS is one-third of CA and CR:CS is the ratio of sphere density to fluid density; erect perpendiculars and construct any hyperbola with asymptote CR; choose CT and the area-cut CZ; then the motion the globe loses traversing CZ is to its entire initial motion approximately as CT is to CR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses analogy to a cylinder and reflections: motion lost by cylinder from reflecting particles relates to mass of fluid displaced; because sphere is 2/3 of cylinder and its resistance is half a cylinder's (previous prop), deduce proportionality of lost motion to Ct/CR. Corollaries: given initial speed one can find the time to lose a given portion of motion; if particles reflect perfectly elastically or perfectly inelastically extremes of resistance follow (twice smaller resistance if no reflection), and intermediate reflectivity gives intermediate resistance; knowledge of resistance for very fast bodies helps deduce resistance for slow bodies if the law of decrease with velocity is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVII (Problem IX) — motion of water efflux from a vessel through an orifice
rubrics_metrics.description: If a vessel filled with water has a hole in its bottom, the motion (momentum) of the water efflux equals that which the weight of the column of water perpendicular to the orifice could generate; equivalently, the efflux velocity relates to the depth of water above the orifice by a geometrical relation: the efflux velocity compared to the velocity V a free-falling body would acquire in time T falling through S is in the ratio d:e where d/e = sqrt(½A : S) (i.e., velocity scales with a mean proportional between the head and the free-fall distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton derives that the total impulse (momentum) of efflux in a given time equals the weight of the column whose base equals the orifice and height equals the water-column above the orifice (Torricelli-like result). He sets symbols F (area of orifice), A (height of water above orifice), etc., and equates generated momentum AF×V to the momentum of efflux, yielding relations dd:ee :: A:2S and thus the velocity of efflux compared to free-fall. Consequences: if the efflux is turned upward, the jet will rise to half the height of the water above the orifice; an oblique jet in nonresisting space describes a parabola whose parameter equals the head height; caveat: for non-very-subtle (viscous) fluids the efflux is slower than the ideal formula, especially through narrow orifices. Also notes that for a horizontal canal outlet the vessel still sustains the full weight of contained water even while efflux occurs, although the side whence the water issues will not sustain the local pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXVIII (Theorem XXIX) — resistance on the front surface of spheres in any fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider flow through a cylindrical channel with a sphere suspended in it: the quantity of water passing per time is proportional to the effective area available to flow (space between sphere and canal), so the velocity of flow when the sphere is present cannot exceed that when it is absent; hence the resistance (or constriction effect) caused by the sphere is governed by the geometrical aperture around it and by the subtlety (viscosity/particulate nature) of the fluid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: place a globe in a cylindrical channel and compare defluxion when sphere removed (channel aperture) vs present (annular space). Using the efflux proposition and assuming a very fluid (subtle) medium, the flow is proportional to aperture area and cannot be greater with the sphere present. If the fluid is not ideally subtle (has coarser particles), transit through narrow gaps is slower and the sphere impedes more. This proposition frames practical estimation of the anterior-surface resistance on spheres in channels and relates to earlier scalings of resistance with aperture and fluid properties.
